opportunities.name: Firm AI Adoption Hit 42% in 2026 — Governance Policy Coverage Didn’t Keep Up
opportunities.problem: Firm-level generative-AI adoption rose from 26% in 2024 to 42% in 2026, but a large share of firms using AI tools still have no formal governance policy, even though ABA Formal Opinion 512 (July 29, 2024) already mapped the existing Model Rules onto generative-AI use and nine states have since issued their own bar guidance on top of it.
opportunities.target_customer: Managing partners and general counsel at small-to-midsize firms (10–150 attorneys) using AI tools without a documented policy.
opportunities.proposed_product: AI Use Policy Pack — a jurisdiction-aware policy template mapped to ABA Formal Opinion 512 plus the applicable state bar opinion, with a one-page staff training summary.
why_now: ABA Formal Opinion 512 (July 29, 2024) already supplies the ethical baseline — competence, confidentiality, fees, supervision — so the gap is adoption of existing guidance, not waiting on new rules.
Nine jurisdictions now layer their own numbered bar opinions on top of the ABA baseline as of 2026, so a single generic template is no longer defensible.
Firm AI adoption crossed 42% in 2026 while formal governance policy coverage lagged well behind — a measurable, publicly reported gap.
opportunities.status_reason: The regulatory baseline is unusually stable (an 18-month-old ABA opinion, not a moving target), and the adoption-versus-governance gap is a durable, quantified number rather than a one-time news spike. Competition is real — several vendors and bar associations already publish free templates — so the opportunity is jurisdiction-specific mapping and delivery, not the base content.

evidence.note: ABA’s own introduction to Formal Opinion 512 (issued July 29, 2024), mapping competence, confidentiality, fees and supervision onto generative-AI use.
A state bar association telling its own members they need this — the buyer’s own professional association articulating the pain point.
A legal-AI vendor already tracking the state-by-state patchwork, evidence the market is actively organizing information around this gap.
An established legaltech vendor already selling into this exact governance gap — direct competitive evidence.
